Family Health

Deep, painful acne: treatment beyond a new cleanser

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Deep, painful acne often needs more than a change of cleanser. A tailored treatment plan can reduce inflammation and scarring while making room for your health history, pregnancy plans and the way acne affects everyday life.

Why deep acne needs a different approach

Acne develops in hair follicles when oil and shed skin cells contribute to blockage and inflammation. The skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes is involved, but acne does not mean that someone is dirty. Scrubbing harder cannot wash a deep inflamed lump away.

The term cystic acne is often used for severe acne with deep, painful lesions. A clinician may distinguish firm nodules from softer cyst-like lesions. These are not simply large surface whiteheads, and other types of acne can also be inflamed. Early treatment matters because deep lesions are more likely to leave lasting scars.

Recognising the pattern

Deep bumps may feel tender or painful before they are obvious. Some become swollen, red or darker than the surrounding skin; others have a pus-filled centre. They can resemble boils, but not every painful lump is acne. A lump that changes rapidly, has spreading redness or accompanies fever should be assessed rather than squeezed.

The face is a common site, but acne can involve the chest, back, neck, shoulders and upper arms. Lesions near or behind the ears may need an examination to confirm the cause. Acne affects different skin types: oily skin can be part of the picture, but dry or combination skin does not rule it out.

Age and hormones do not tell the whole story

Acne is common in adolescence and can persist or first appear in adulthood. Some people notice flares around their periods. Hormonal influences matter, but adult acne does not automatically mean a hormone disorder or a measurable hormonal imbalance.

Tell the clinician about irregular periods, new excess facial hair, medicines and any pregnancy plans. These details may change the assessment. Acne may improve with age, but waiting for that to happen is not a good plan when lesions are painful, scarring or affecting confidence and daily life.

A treatment plan takes time

Over-the-counter products may help some acne but often do not control deep, persistent lesions on their own. A clinician can assess severity, scarring and the effect on wellbeing, then choose treatment or arrange dermatology referral. The plan may combine medicines that act in different ways.

Improvement usually takes several weeks rather than a few days. Early irritation and a lack of immediate clearing do not necessarily mean treatment has failed. Agree on when to review progress, how to use each product and which reactions mean seeking advice sooner. Repeatedly adding new strong products can make irritation worse.

When oral isotretinoin may be considered

Isotretinoin is an oral retinoid related to vitamin A. It can be highly effective for severe acne, especially when there is a risk of scarring or other appropriate treatments have not worked. Accutane is a familiar brand name, but available brands and prescribing arrangements vary.

The dose and length of treatment are individual decisions. A statement that a fixed percentage of people will clear within four to six months cannot promise your result. Some people need a different course length or further treatment later. Isotretinoin should be prescribed with follow-up and monitoring, not obtained as a stronger version of an ordinary skin supplement.

Pregnancy prevention and monitoring with isotretinoin

Isotretinoin can seriously harm a developing baby and must not be used during pregnancy. Anyone who could become pregnant needs the locally required pregnancy-prevention and testing plan before treatment begins. Protection is needed before, during and after treatment; the prescribing team must explain the timing and what to do after a missed period or possible pregnancy.

Discuss breastfeeding, liver problems, blood-fat levels, mental health history and all other medicines or supplements. Regular reviews and selected blood tests are part of care. Vitamin A supplements and certain antibiotics can interact with isotretinoin. Do not combine treatments or change the dose without checking with the prescriber.

Separate common side effects from warning signs

Dry lips, skin, eyes and nasal passages are common with isotretinoin; nasal dryness can cause nosebleeds. Skin may become irritated or more sun-sensitive, and muscle or joint aches can occur. Ask about suitable moisturiser, lip care and any changes to exercise. Report troublesome symptoms instead of assuming every reaction is unavoidable.

Persistent severe headache, especially with vomiting or visual disturbance, needs urgent advice; medicine leaflets advise stopping isotretinoin and obtaining urgent assessment for this pattern. Unexplained bruising, blood in the urine, severe abdominal pain or bloody diarrhoea also needs prompt medical attention. A severe allergic reaction, breathing difficulty or immediate risk of self-harm requires emergency help.

Report new or worsening depression, anxiety or other mental health changes promptly. The relationship between isotretinoin, mood and inflammatory bowel disease is more complex than a list implying that it inevitably causes these conditions. Uncertainty about causation is not a reason to ignore symptoms. The prescriber should discuss relevant warnings and monitor your experience throughout treatment.

Oral antibiotics have a defined role

An oral antibiotic may be used for moderate or severe inflammatory acne, particularly when a larger area is affected. It can reduce bacterial activity and inflammation, but does not address every part of pore blockage or oil production. It is usually part of a combined plan rather than a long-term stand-alone solution.

Courses should be reviewed and limited to reduce antibiotic resistance. Guidance recommends combining systemic antibiotics with benzoyl peroxide and other suitable topical treatment. The exact combination depends on tolerance and circumstances; this is not an instruction to add those products to an isotretinoin regimen.

Possible effects depend on the antibiotic and can include nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, vomiting and sun sensitivity. Pregnancy, age, allergies and other medicines affect selection. If treatment is not helping, seek a review rather than extending or repeating leftover antibiotics yourself.

Topical retinoids help keep follicles from blocking

Topical retinoids act on how skin cells turn over and help reduce blocked follicles. They do not detach the hair follicle from the skin. Examples used for acne include adapalene and tretinoin, with some tazarotene preparations also used. Availability without a prescription differs by country and formulation.

Brand names are not interchangeable treatment instructions. Differin contains adapalene; Retin-A and Avita are tretinoin products, and Tazorac is a tazarotene brand. Avage is also tazarotene, but its US indication concerns signs of facial photoageing rather than making every tazarotene cream an acne product. Ask a pharmacist to confirm the ingredient, strength and approved use.

Using a retinoid without overwhelming the skin

Creams, gels and lotions differ in how they feel and how easily they irritate skin. Redness, dryness, peeling or stinging can occur, especially early on. The clinician may adjust the frequency or application method. More product or more frequent application does not guarantee faster improvement.

Use sun protection and avoid piling on abrasive scrubs or several irritating treatments. A retinoid may be combined with other prescribed acne treatments, but topical antibiotics also need resistance-conscious prescribing. Discuss pregnancy before use: topical retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy and when planning it. An oral isotretinoin capsule and a retinoid cream do not have identical risk profiles.

Spironolactone can help selected adults

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic also used for conditions such as high blood pressure. Its antiandrogen action can help persistent acne in selected women. A jawline or menstrual-flare pattern can be relevant, but benefit is not restricted to acne in one exact location. It is not routinely used for male acne because of its hormonal side effects.

Possible effects include breast tenderness, irregular periods, dizziness, headache, tiredness and more frequent urination. Potassium can rise, especially with kidney or heart problems or interacting medicines. The prescriber decides which blood-pressure, kidney-function and potassium checks are needed. Avoid it during pregnancy and discuss contraception and pregnancy plans.

Spironolactone research is not a self-dosing guide

A 2012 clinical review described doses and experience from earlier studies; it was not a single trial proving one best dose for everyone. It does not justify routinely exceeding 200 mg daily or claiming that higher doses reduce side effects. Dose changes belong with the prescribing clinician.

The later SAFA randomised trial studied adult women with persistent facial acne. Outcomes favoured spironolactone, with a clearer difference at twenty-four weeks than at twelve weeks. This supports its role as an option and shows why follow-up takes time. It does not mean every person with deep acne should receive it or will have the same response.

Combined contraceptive pills are another option for some people

Certain combined oral contraceptives, containing an oestrogen and a progestogen, can improve acne. They may be useful when contraception is also wanted or acne flares around periods. Not every contraceptive pill has the same effect, and a progestogen-only pill is not equivalent to a combined acne treatment.

A clinician must check suitability, including blood-clot history, migraine, smoking, blood pressure and other health factors. Pregnancy intentions also matter. Do not start or switch a pill solely because another person’s skin improved. Ask about expected bleeding changes, side effects and when the skin response will be reviewed.

Treat active acne before planning scar procedures

Avoid squeezing, picking or attempting to drain deep lesions. Trauma can intensify inflammation, introduce infection and increase scarring. It does not follow that every squeezed mild spot becomes cystic acne, and leaving a spot alone cannot guarantee that no scar will form. Effective control of active acne is the more useful long-term aim.

Once acne is controlled, a dermatologist can assess the type of scarring and discuss options. Chemical peels, dermabrasion and laser resurfacing are different procedures, with different depths, recovery periods and risks. They may improve selected scars but cannot promise completely unmarked skin.

Skin tone, scar shape, previous treatments and medicines affect the choice and timing. Pigment changes, infection or further scarring are possible complications. Do not perform deep peels or use an abrasive device on inflamed cysts at home. Discuss procedural timing carefully if using or recently completing isotretinoin.

Keep everyday care gentle and realistic

Use a gentle cleanser, generally twice a day and after substantial sweating, without repeated harsh washing or scrubbing. Remove make-up before bed. Choose moisturiser, make-up and sunscreen labelled non-comedogenic, meaning formulated not to clog pores. Oily-looking skin can still need moisturiser when treatment causes dryness.

Use broad-spectrum sun protection suited to your skin, along with shade and clothing. Sunscreen is not something to avoid because some products feel greasy; select a tolerable formulation. After exercise, change out of sweaty clothing and cleanse gently rather than rubbing vigorously.

Stress can accompany or worsen acne for some people, but it is not a personal failure or a complete explanation for severe disease. Research has explored high-glycaemic eating patterns, yet banning bread, rice or pasta is not an established cure. Aim for balanced meals and discuss concerns instead of starting a restrictive diet. Skincare and lifestyle support treatment; they cannot reliably prevent every deep lesion.

Make follow-up part of the plan

Ask what to do if a product irritates, a dose is missed or a deep lesion becomes especially painful. A dermatologist may offer a targeted procedure, such as an injection for a selected inflamed lesion, but routine surgery is not required for every case of cystic acne.

Treatment often needs adjustment over weeks or months. Once improved, some people benefit from a maintenance plan to reduce relapse. Return sooner for new scarring, worsening pain or substantial distress. Getting help early is reasonable even if acne has not reached its most severe form.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prescription choices and combinations depend on acne severity, scarring, tolerance and individual risks. Treatment response takes time.

Retinoid and hormonal treatment advice needs pregnancy planning, medicine checks and appropriate monitoring. Historical response figures are not individual guarantees.

How BeMama can help

Bring a list of skin products and medicines, photographs of flares if helpful, and the concerns you most want treatment to address.

When to seek help

Dermatology review and country-specific prescribing and pregnancy-prevention checks remain pending. This article does not provide a self-prescribing schedule.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Deep lesions deserve assessment before scarring accumulates.
  • Isotretinoin requires pregnancy precautions and monitoring.
  • Antibiotic and hormonal treatment choices are individual.
  • Gentle care supports treatment without replacing it.

Frequently asked questions

Does cystic acne mean my skin is dirty?

No. Follicle blockage and inflammation are involved. Harsh cleansing can irritate skin without treating a deep lesion.

Can I have deep acne without very oily skin?

Yes. Skin type alone does not establish or exclude acne. A clinician can check a painful or unusual lump.

Should I wait until I grow out of it?

Pain, new scars or distress are reasons to seek help now. Improvement with age is not guaranteed.

Will isotretinoin definitely clear my acne in four to six months?

No fixed time or percentage can guarantee your response. Course length and follow-up are individual.

Can I use isotretinoin when trying for a baby?

No. It can seriously harm a developing baby. Follow the prescribing team’s pregnancy-prevention and stopping-time instructions.

Is every headache while taking isotretinoin harmless?

No. Persistent severe headache, especially with vomiting or vision changes, needs urgent advice. Stop the medicine and seek urgent assessment for that pattern, as directed in its leaflet.

Does a higher spironolactone dose mean fewer side effects?

No. That is not a safe interpretation of the evidence. The dose and monitoring must be chosen by the prescriber.

Are all retinoid brands interchangeable?

No. Ingredient, strength, formulation and approved use differ. Some similarly named products are intended for photoageing rather than acne.

Must I cut out rice, bread and pasta?

A blanket ban is not an established acne treatment. Aim for balanced meals and discuss a suspected pattern without adopting a restrictive diet.

Can scar treatment replace control of active acne?

No. New lesions can create new scars. First control active acne, then discuss procedures matched to the scars and skin.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
